First, it extracts the `selector` strings from the `usesSchema` definitions and evaluates them using a native Go label-matching engine (supporting Kubernetes-style `AND`, `OR` via `in()`, and `NOT` via `!=` semantics) across the explicitly defined graph edges to guarantee cross-node type safety over **declared** sockets. An edge on an ad-hoc socket — one an Aggregate author named and the catalog did not declare — has no catalog entry and therefore no selector, so there is nothing for this check to evaluate and nothing missing; each edge records which of the two it is, and what an ad-hoc edge may carry is bounded by the target's declared `provides` instead. It also evaluates Feature `appliesTo` and `appliesToAnyOf` selectors to verify that attached features are compatible with their target component's labels, and each filled attachment slot's own `selector` against the labels of the Feature filling it. Second, it evaluates every **presence mandate** a node's Component declares — each `features.aggrega.ai/requiredType.<label>` annotation — against that node's final attachment set. The analyzer is where this check belongs because it is the first stage that holds both halves of the rule: the resolved Component entity's annotations and the attachment set the 5-Tier cascade produced, counting Aggregate-attached, subsystem-attached, Release-attached and annotation-expanded attachments alike. A mandate no attachment satisfies halts the build; a mandate whose declaration is malformed halts with a distinct diagnostic, so a broken declaration never reads as a satisfied requirement. Third, it executes the **Validation Gate**, passing the complete graph structure (including all nodes, edges, attached features, and precalculated DFS paths) to a governance plugin attached at the `ir-verdict` role. The enterprise's custom Wasm policy evaluates the topology. If the Wasm plugin returns a failure array (e.g., detecting a continuous path from a `public` node to a `restricted` node without a specific proxy feature), the build halts.

The schema answer and the enumeration are never combined, so which question was answered is readable from the response. So each value is spelled before it becomes a directory or file name — a lowercase letter, a digit, `.`, `_` and `-` are written as they are, and every other character is written as an escape opening with `+`. `core/devtool/adminer:1.0.0` at version `1.0.0` is the slot `entities/core+zsdevtool+zsadminer+zx00003a1.0.0/1.0.0/`, and a slot named by a content digest is `sha256+zx00003a<hex>`. An uppercase letter is escaped too, so two coordinates differing only in letter case keep two slots on a file system that ignores case; a name Windows reserves for a device, such as `con`, has its first letter escaped; and no name ends in a full stop. Two different values never share a name, and one value has the same name on every machine. `aggrega cache status` lists each entry by the values its names were spelled from — a catalog entity by its coordinate and version — rather than by the spelled names.

Detection reads only the source you sent — of a directory, only the files a signature's file patterns select — and no network, parsing each file it reads through the parser the workspace's catalog serves for a syntax — or, for a syntax the catalog serves no parser for, the one the compiler itself carries — once for each syntax a signature applying to its name reads it in; the importer then reads the source through the same parser. A signature declaring no file pattern applies to the file you sent whatever it is called, and to no file of a directory; the Langflow, Flowise and n8n importers' signatures are of that kind and read JSON, and the Dify importer's reads YAML, so recognising a file you sent on its own reads it as JSON and as YAML, which needs no parser in the workspace's catalog: the compiler carries a JSON and a YAML parser, and one the catalog serves is used in its place. A source no signature matches is refused asking for `format` and naming the formats the importers advertise, under the condition [No importer recognises the source](../errors/fatal-halts.md#no-importer-recognises-the-source); a source signatures of more than one format match is refused naming them, under the condition [More than one importer recognises the source](../errors/fatal-halts.md#more-than-one-importer-recognises-the-source). Each refusal's `data` carries its condition's `code` and `shortCode`, so a client asks for the format on the code rather than on the words. Neither is guessed at, because a guessed format resolves the wrong importer and produces confident nonsense. `format` in the response is the one that was used, detected or named, so a client that omitted it learns what it got.

A token failing any of those is answered `401`, with `error="invalid_token"` added to the same challenge a caller carrying nothing receives — and the answer is identical whichever check turned it away, so a caller learns that it needs a different token rather than which part of the one it sent was wrong. Masking is not prevention. Under `redact`, as here, the gateway refuses no request for the sensitive text it finds in it — what it refuses is what its masking does not reach; text no pattern matches and the recognizer does not detect passes unchanged; the names of the keys in tool-call arguments, tool results and the caller's metadata are not masked; the developer's own definitions — tools, a response format, stop sequences — and the reasoning of an earlier turn that a client sends back pass as sent; the gateway and the two recognizer services see the original text, and what the gateway records about a call — in its own log, or in what it hands a logging integration — can still hold it; and traffic that does not pass through the gateway is not touched. The FeatureRecipe's comments beside its `write_request_policy` step list what this gateway refuses and what it passes on as sent.

174b4c3b529b0bd1: **A path a call names stays inside that workspace too.** Over HTTP a path argument is resolved against the workspace root and refused if it reaches outside it — a relative path that climbs out of the workspace, an absolute path naming somewhere else, and a relative path leading out of the workspace through a link to a file or a directory that is there, each come back as a failure naming the argument, and naming neither the workspace root nor the place the path would have reached; a relative path is quoted back as you sent it. Every path argument is judged by where it leads, by the definition of inside [The workspace boundary](workspace-boundary.md#what-lies-inside-the-workspace) states, whether the tool reads it or writes it — the directory `gen-catalog` writes its output into, the document `edit-document` writes back and the entity `pin` writes its lock beside as much as a document a tool reads — so a path not made yet beneath a link leading out of the workspace is refused as that link is, with nothing read or written. A `release` naming a Release the served workspace's configuration names, as `build.authoring_release` or as a key of `workspace.releases`, is reached through that configuration and is accepted through a link wherever its file sits; no other argument has that exception. Where the path you meant is inside that workspace but was spelled absolutely, the refusal gives you the root-relative spelling to send instead, so a caller that guessed the wrong form is told the right one rather than only that it was wrong. That holds for the paths a call names as its subject — the document to validate, the Release to build, the directory a generation writes its output into — and for the ones a tool writes to no less than the ones it reads: a caller reaching a server over the network is asking a machine it cannot see to read and write files, and the workspace the operator chose is where that reading and writing is kept. Over standard input and output each tool's path arguments keep the contract described under that tool below, where a path may be absolute and may point outside the workspace — the person calling owns the machine the server is running on, so confining them to a directory they chose themselves would buy nothing. The two tools whose operation itself answers only about a document the workspace carries, `insertion-point` and `edit-document`, keep that on both transports, and refuse a document outside the workspace whether it is written that way or reached through a link leading out of it. What is honoured over standard input and output is the path a call names and nothing beyond it. What the operation then reads and writes on its own account is held on both transports exactly as it is when the same command is typed at a terminal: a walk or a lookup does not read through a link leading out of the workspace, a file a Release in the workspace or its Manifest names by a path is not read from outside the workspace — and one a Release the call named outside the workspace names is not read from outside the directory holding that Release — and a file written beneath a directory — the workspace, or one the call named — stays inside that directory. [The workspace boundary](workspace-boundary.md#the-two-assistant-transports) sets the two transports beside the command line and the editor, and states what remains open over standard input and output: a document in a workspace you cloned can steer an assistant into naming a path outside the workspace, and that path is honoured as named.

Its `executionScope: boundary` runs the FR once per parent-boundary attachment. The per-(path, provider) compose assembler merges the gateway alongside the per-component contributors at the same evaluated path: one `docker-compose.yaml` containing every component plus the bridge gateway. 25bd4fc5e876a65f: **Higress in front of models:** `core/gateway/higress`, the open-source Higress gateway, built on Envoy and configured through Kubernetes resources, serves the models wired to its own `models` socket through Higress's AI proxy. Its one realization is a chart Recipe over the project's own `higress-core` Helm chart, which runs Higress's controller, with its discovery service, and the gateway; there is no compose realization, since the project means its compose distribution mainly for local testing and that distribution runs several cooperating services configured through a store of their own. The Recipe pins the chart, the images and every plugin module it writes, and accepts in `infra.source_version` only the chart versions its configuration is proven at; the gateway fetches those modules from the Higress plugin registry at run time, which the cluster must reach and the build cannot check. The controller watches only the Release's namespace, under an IngressClass named for the gateway and that namespace, so two Higress gateways in one namespace collide. Each alias gets a route at `/<alias>/v1`, sent to the `endpoint` the alias's model publishes through an entry of the gateway's own registry and asking for the `model` it publishes whatever model name a request carries, so the path chooses the model; connections naming one alias in their `serves` value share its requests in equal shares. The gateway presents each connection's own credential as a bearer token, which the Higress controller reads from the Secret the AI proxy's configuration names, in the gateway's namespace, and hands the gateway, so the key is in no rendered file; a Secret name holding a dot halts the build, since Higress reads the name up to its first dot, and a connection carrying no credential passes on the key the request presents. Higress's AI proxy also copies the `Authorization` header a client sends into an `X-HI-ORIGINAL-AUTH` header, and every model route removes that copy before the request reaches the model, so a key a client presents never travels beside a connection's own credential. Over https the gateway checks that a model's certificate chains to the system's trust anchors and names the model's host, whatever host the client sent, and sends the model nothing otherwise: the Recipe marks the route of every alias whose connections are all https with Higress's `higress.io/backend-protocol: HTTPS` annotation, so the gateway takes the server name from the host the AI proxy writes into each request — the model's, qualified with the model's namespace where it carries no dot — and checks the certificate against it. That annotation applies to every connection of an alias, so an alias mixing http and https connections halts the build, naming both; serving them under two aliases clears it. A connection reaching a model whose `model.aggrega.ai/api` is not `openai`, or whose endpoint names an address rather than a host, halts the build. It publishes the route of the alias its `values.model` names as its `endpoint` and that alias as its `model`, and carries `model.aggrega.ai/api: openai`, so an agent's `model` socket takes it as it takes the AI gateway; with nothing wired it publishes both keys empty. It declares no callers, so its model routes check no caller's key, and a value needing a caller the gateway verified is refused by name. Of the controls below it realizes the period budget, audit logging and the retry policy, each written onto the model routes, and it realizes `core/data-masking` as "Data Exfiltration & Payload Interception" below describes. Its realizations of response validation, the fallback chain, the semantic cache, prompt-injection screening and target selection halt every attachment, each naming why, and neither prompt deny patterns nor the concurrency limit attaches to it, since it carries no `dataplane.aggrega.ai/prompt-guard` or `dataplane.aggrega.ai/concurrency-cap` value. That a running gateway enforces any of these controls is not observed by any build.

The compiler evaluates nested modules and resolves them down into a flat, 1-dimensional Intermediate Representation (IR) graph before passing the data to the Wasm rendering plugins. Crucially, while the graph is flattened, the compiler perfectly preserves **Feature Atomicity**. If a proxy feature autonomously declares a network edge to a secure vault, the compiler records the semantic origin of that edge, ensuring Wasm policy engines can execute $O(1)$ lookups without falsely attributing the connection to the parent component. Finally, to support temporal sequencing, each boundary in the Release carries a `syncWave: <integer>` value; each rendering plugin translates the per-boundary wave into whatever its own target expresses ordering with — an execution-order annotation the downstream GitOps controller reads, or a dependency between the services of the file it renders — while a target with no ordering surface at all records the wave without sequencing on it.

3442c41536cf755e: **Prompt-injection screening:** `core/prompt-injection-shield` declares that the model requests a gateway forwards are checked, before the model is called, for an attempt to override the instructions the model was given, at a `sensitivity` of `standard` or `strict` — strict refusing more such attempts, and more legitimate requests with them. The check is a probabilistic classifier's verdict: it misses some attacks — reworded, encoded or respelled ones among them — refuses some legitimate requests, and is known to be evadable, so it is one control beside others, and it does not judge the model's reply, tool-call arguments or images. It attaches to any gateway, and a realization either sends the gateway's requests through a guard wired to its `guard` socket, which needs nothing of the gateway but that it forwards to an address it is configured with, or turns on a check the gateway runs itself. Through a guard, the guard checks each request and forwards what it admits to the model, and attaching the Feature with nothing on that socket halts the build naming it. The standard library realizes it on the AI gateway and on the NGINX gateway, each with `core/security/nemo-guardrails` as the guard: a service speaking the OpenAI chat-completions API, whose rail sends the latest user message of a request to the classifier of the `core/security/trustyai-huggingface-detector` wired to it and refuses the request when that classifier's score reaches the guard's threshold. A refused request is answered by the guard itself, with an ordinary completion, and nothing of it reaches the model; when the guard or its detector cannot be reached the request is refused too. Each of the two halts the build unless the guard is that one, running the threshold the sensitivity names — 0.5 for `standard` and 0.001 for `strict`, the two values measured for the detector's default classifier, which the gateway, seeing the guard and not the detector behind it, cannot check the model of. On the AI gateway every alias of the model map is sent to the guard, each target written `openai/<model>`, so the map is the one typed by hand: a model wired to the gateway's `models` socket would be sent to its own endpoint with its own connection's credential, past the guard, and the realization halts the build while that socket holds a connection, naming it. The AI gateway refuses every request but a chat completion, the one kind the guard checks; on the NGINX gateway its one location forwards to the guard in place of the upstream, and the guard answers no other model route. On `core/gateway/azure-api-management` it is realized as Azure's own prompt shield, turned on in the API's policy through the instance's Azure AI Content Safety backend that `infra.content_safety_backend_id` names, and the build halts while that key is unset: Azure AI Content Safety checks each request for a user attack before the model is called, ahead of a semantic cache's lookup, and the gateway answers one it detects with HTTP 403, as it answers a request longer than the service accepts. The shield is on or off, so `standard` is kept and `strict` is refused by name, and it runs at Microsoft's own sensitivity, not measured against the threshold `standard` names on the guards. The instance reaches that backend with its managed identity, which needs the Cognitive Services User role on the service; the build sees neither. No gateway in the standard library but these three realizes it, and attaching it to another halts the build naming the type: most render no route a realization could send through a guard — they keep their routes in a store of their own, take them from the services behind them, or are a hosted service on which the standard library turns on no check of this kind — and `core/gateway/apisix`, whose chart Recipe renders the routes of the models wired to it, and `core/gateway/envoy-gateway`, whose Recipe renders the AI route of the models wired to it, have no realization of it. On `core/gateway/agentgateway`, whose Recipes render an entry for each model wired to it, the realization halts every attachment, naming why: agentgateway judges a request for such an attempt only through a service it calls — a webhook the operator runs, or Azure AI Content Safety, Google Model Armor or AWS Bedrock Guardrails — and the realization wires none of them. On `core/gateway/higress` the realization halts every attachment too, naming why: Higress judges such an attempt only through a service it calls — Alibaba Cloud's content-security service, or, through a plugin its source carries but its 2.2.5 plugin release does not publish, a Qwen3Guard model service the operator runs — each letting the request through when that call fails, and the realization wires neither. On `core/gateway/traefik-hub` the realization halts every attachment as well, naming why: Traefik Hub judges such an attempt only through a service it calls — its LLM Guard and Parallel LLM Guard middlewares, which call a guard service or a model in a request and with conditions the realization would have to write, and whose work with a prompt-attack detector is not measured, so no sensitivity maps to a check there; or its Azure Prompt Shield, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and GCP Model Armor middlewares, which call hosted services the realization does not wire. The guard reads only the latest user message, so a system message, an earlier turn or a tool result reaches the model unread, and only traffic crossing the gateway is screened: a workload calling the model's address directly goes around it.

3a1779d74a2141b5: **A flow is drafted as the platform that runs it.** A Langflow flow, a Flowise chatflow and an n8n workflow run on a platform, and by default an import drafts that platform rather than the flow's nodes: one instance of the standard library's platform Component — `core/ai-agent/langflow`, `core/ai-agent/flowise` or `core/ai-agent/n8n` — carrying the flow as it was exported in its `flow_definition` value, which the platform loads at deploy. Each part of the flow a socket of the platform takes — on the standard library's platforms, a model, an MCP server or another tool reached over HTTP, and a vector store — becomes a Component of its own, referenced or drafted as the mapping decides, and is wired to that socket under the platform's `uses`. So each call the flow makes to a model, a tool or a store is a connection the Aggregate declares: a governance plugin judging the graph sees it as it sees any other edge, and the standard library's egress allowlist, which the `attach_egress_allowlist` setting attaches to the platform, lets the platform connect only to what its connections reach, its own pods and the cluster's DNS. Where the format lets it, the draft writes into the carried flow what makes the flow reach each part through its connection. Every other node — an agent, a chain, a trigger — stays inside the carried flow and becomes no Component, its decision recording the candidates it was weighed against. A Dify application is drafted the same way, in the form a whole installation takes: one entry of the Dify installation the standard library assembles, `core/dify`, carrying the application in its `app_definition` parameter, the installation wiring its own connections. 465eb6e481f5f514: **The AOT Compiler & Execution Handoff:** A strict compilation pipeline translates the DSL into a capability-agnostic Intermediate Representation (IR) graph. The IR captures the topology of components and the `uses` edges between them (who uses whom); the compiler passes this graph to the WebAssembly (Wasm) governance socket to detect transitive trust vulnerabilities, then executes Wasm rendering plugins to generate the precise proxy and guardrail configurations. Aggrega writes these artifacts to disk and hands off physical deployment to other tools like CI/CD pipelines or runtime orchestrators.

Several gateways here can verify against an anchor, which is why `dataplane.aggrega.ai/upstream-tls: trust-anchor` is a value a selector can match. Pinning is a separate capability, and at least two independent products implement it for the connections they open to an upstream: Tyk takes the upstream's public key in PEM form, and Envoy takes a hash of it. So it is a Feature, `core/upstream-key-pinning`, whose selector names `dataplane.aggrega.ai/upstream-pinning: public-key`, and what this catalog realizes is answered product by product: `core/gateway/tyk` carries the value and a FeatureRecipe for each of its targets, while the gateways here that embed Envoy expose its pin setting only for the certificates clients present, or not at all, so they carry no value and an attachment to them halts at the selector. A pin narrows what an upstream may present; it is a control, not an assurance that the connection is otherwise sound.

**The Deterministic Output Rule (GitOps Safety):**
Because GitOps controllers (ArgoCD, Flux) perform byte-level diff detection on rendered artifacts, the compiler guarantees that identical inputs produce byte-identical outputs. Maps that flow through the template context (`.context.inject.env`, `.values`, `.infra`, and the rest of the runtime view) are backed by ordered-map structures that preserve author insertion order across the data layer; `{{ range }}` over those maps iterates in author order, not in alphabetical order. Ops engineers can rely on iteration order being deterministic across runs of the same input. The Sprig `keys` function, however, returns Go-map iteration order (which is non-deterministic by language design); templates that compose a deterministic key sequence from `keys` output must pipe through `sortAlpha` (e.g., `{{ keys .values | sortAlpha }}`) to recover determinism.

4e36473bfaef51ce: **How to fix:** first find what differs between two builds of the component the message names — build it twice and compare the outputs. Where the difference is a value a chart you source generates afresh on every render — a random password, a generated key, a timestamp in a Secret or a ConfigMap — the fault is in that chart's output rather than in the provider, and you can clear it yourself in one of two ways. Supply the value, through whatever setting the chart offers for it, from the Recipe's `valuesMapping:`, so the chart stops generating it. Or, where the generated document is one the Release must not ship — a Secret the operator supplies separately, say — leave it out of the build with an `omits:` entry on the Recipe; see [Recipe → The `omits:` field](../entities/recipe.md#the-omits-field--leaving-rendered-documents-out-of-a-source). Otherwise the fault is the provider's rather than your documents', and nothing you can write clears it. Report it to whoever publishes the plugin serving that provider, naming the component the message identifies — the usual causes are a timestamp, a random value, or an ordering that follows a map's iteration rather than the order the author wrote. Until it is fixed, the ordinary build mode is unaffected, and pinning the plugin to a version that passed is the practical answer.

4e67c342ea3aa17b: **The Flavored Interfaces (Schema Inheritance):** A Component may declare `extends`, naming another Component as its base, and what that composes is **structure**: labels, annotations, attachment slots, the self-inject allowlist, topology sockets and named `assertions`. The three data pillars do not compose — an extending Component writes the literal marker `schema: inherited` and authors no `values`, `infra` or `provides` content of its own, so its contract is its base's identically. That is why the mechanism **narrows rather than varies**: because the contract is unchanged, every Recipe written for the base already serves the specialization, and the specialization costs one catalog entity and one Manifest mapping line. What a specialization adds is therefore identity a selector or a policy reads — an audit tier, a data zone, a governance contact, or a socket whose selector admits less than the base's. It cannot add a different contract, because it has no surface on which to author one. One consequence is easy to miss: **the mapping line is still required.** Recipe selection is by exact mapping key, so a specialization needs its own `mappings.components.type` entry even though it needs no Recipe of its own. See [examples/extends-wrapper](../language-reference/examples/extends-wrapper/) for a published wrapper that adds a reviewed-tier label and narrows a socket on it, together with the build that halts when an edge wired into that socket leaves the tier. A trait that depends on how a component is configured is **not** this mechanism's subject: a specialization pins its base's artifact and inherits its contract, so a trait true of the specialization is already true of the base, where the Naked Base rule puts it. Such a trait belongs to the Dynamic Mutator below.

The workspace root is the directory of the nearest ancestor `.aggrega-config.yaml`
carrying a `workspace:` block, or the directory `--workspace-root` names. When the
root is pinned this way, a build is **invocation-location-independent**: running
`aggrega build` from the project root and from a subdirectory produces
byte-identical IR and rendered artifacts, because the catalog searched and the
source paths recorded in the output do not shift with the working directory. (With
no `workspace:` marker and no `--workspace-root`, the working directory is the
root, so output is anchored there instead — unless the working directory anchors
nothing and `--release` names the Release by an absolute path: the root is then
discovered again from the Release's own folder, so the catalog searched and the
paths recorded in the output are those of the project the Release belongs to,
wherever you run the command from. See
[configuration.md](configuration.md#the-other-ways-a-project-root-is-recognised).)
Where no workspace is found that way either and nothing names one, the build says on
standard error which folder it used as the root, and a build asked to resolve its
dependencies first is refused before anything is fetched, because the cache that
resolution fills would be written in that folder and make it a workspace. A build that
resolves nothing first still renders, but for the same reason an external input the
lockfile pins and the cache no longer holds is not fetched again: the plugin that asks
for it is told the refusal's sentence in its place, as it is told the offline posture's,
and the build reports what that plugin makes of it. A
`--workspace-root` or `AGGREGA_WORKSPACE_ROOT` naming a folder that does not exist is
refused before the build does anything else, naming whichever of the two supplied it.

5d39032662e99f6e: `aggrega build` follows the Single Entry Point Principle: the Release is the sole compilation input. `aggrega build --release release.yaml` reads the Release's `aggregate:` and `manifest:` pointers to locate the rest of the topology, and produces per-boundary output under `dist/`: a named boundary renders under its declared `directory:`, or under `dist/boundaries/<boundary-name>/` when it declares none; a Release that declares top-level `components:` instead of named boundaries renders flat under `dist/`. Every component the topology holds must belong to one of those boundaries, and a component none of them holds halts the build: a component reaches a boundary either by being named under that boundary's `components:`, under the id it carries once sub-Aggregates are flattened, or by sitting inside a sub-Aggregate the boundary routes in under `aggregates:`. A component reaching neither would render outside every boundary the Release declares, taking its output location, sync wave, annotations and per-component `infra:` from nowhere, so the build stops and names the component rather than emitting artifacts the Release's boundary configuration was never applied to. The same relation is checked from the Release's side: a boundary entry naming a component the topology does not hold configures nothing, so it halts too and the diagnostic reports the id the entry addressed. `aggrega inspect` and `aggrega pull` share the Release-as-input shape; `aggrega push` takes a catalog entity; `aggrega validate` and `aggrega lint` accept a catalog entity, a Release (via `--release`), or the whole catalog; `aggrega serve` runs as a long-lived process. 5e90a8f46f14d499: **How to fix:** re-resolve the release and commit the rewritten lockfile. For everything a build reports, a plain `aggrega pull --release <release>` — the command the build prints — is the whole fix: it resolves the release as it now stands, rewrites the pins that moved and holds every other one, so nothing floats that you did not touch. Where what moved is a file under a Recipe's or FeatureRecipe's local source, that pull first halts naming `aggrega pin` for the entity, because recording the new pin beside it is the author's step; run it, or pass `--pin-sources` to the pull, and the pull clears the drift. The one entry a plain pull does not clear is a source reference that moved at its remote, because clearing it means adopting the commit the reference names now: `aggrega pull --upgrade --release <release>` does that, and the entry says so — where the Recipe's `entity.lock` records that source, the upgrade halts the same way until the new commit is pinned beside it. Read the entries before you do, because the third shape is the one worth pausing on: a reference the release no longer reaches is usually a dependency you removed on purpose, but where you did not remove it, something else changed that made it unreachable. A pair that moved on a reference you did not touch means the content at that version is not the content that was reviewed, which is a question for whoever supplies it rather than something to adopt without looking.

65aefd1281b9c98d: **A required signature the lockfile does not record.** Where the trust configuration requires a signature for a dependency the cache serves and the lockfile row records none — the row was edited, the lockfile was written afresh over a cache an earlier pull filled, or the requirement was added after the pull that wrote the row — the re-pull asks that dependency's registry for its signature, by the digest of the manifest stored beside it in the cache, exactly as it does for a dependency it fetches, and records the verified signature on the row. That row is the one a build refuses ([No verified signature is recorded for an artifact that requires one](../errors/fatal-halts.md#no-verified-signature-is-recorded-for-an-artifact-that-requires-one)), so pulling again is what clears that refusal. A registry that attaches no signature, or a signature the trust configuration does not accept, halts the re-pull as it halts a pull that fetched the dependency. The settings that let a pull admit a dependency with no signature leave such a row as it is and ask nothing about it: `skip_signature_verification` at the top level, the same switch on the registry's own entry except for a kind the workspace-wide signing policy requires, and a registry marked `advisory`.
65b35a0560177f19: `aggrega/irGraph` — the compiled IR graph for a Release, for editor introspection. `release` is a path relative to the workspace root, naming a Release inside it — the same value `aggrega build --release` takes when run from the root. Any other form is refused with the standard invalid-params error naming what to send instead: an absolute path, a path that resolves outside the workspace root — whether it climbs out as written or leads out through a link, to the file or to a directory on the way — and an empty value are all rejected rather than resolved, so a request never reports on a file the workspace does not hold. A Release your workspace configuration names, as `build.authoring_release` or as a key of `workspace.releases`, is one the workspace holds wherever its file sits, so a link inside the workspace leading to it is accepted, as `aggrega/releaseCandidates` lists it. A catalog directory the Release reads that cannot be walked — one that is there and cannot be read, say — is refused as [`aggrega inspect`](aggrega-inspect.md) refuses it, before anything else is read: the error is `1004` entity-not-resolvable, its message is the report the command line prints for that directory, on one line (`[CATALOG_ERROR] <directory>: catalog load: …`), and no graph is drawn over the directories that remain. A directory the workspace configuration lists where nothing exists is not refused: it is read as holding nothing, as every command reads it ([Where local entities are read from](configuration.md#where-local-entities-are-read-from)), and the graph is the one drawn without it. A catalog directory holding a link that leads out of the directory its reads must stay inside — a document or a directory linked from elsewhere, beneath a catalog directory inside the workspace or beneath one the configuration names outside it — is refused the same way and at the same moment, with `1004` and the condition's own sentence naming the link and where it leads: nothing is read through such a link, and a graph drawn without it could resolve another entity of the same name in its place. So is a link leading out among the documents beside the Release, where the Release names its Aggregate or its Manifest by identity. A file the Release, its Manifest or a Release it extends names by a path — `aggregate:`, `manifest:`, `extends:` or a parameters `$import:` — that leads out of the workspace, as written or through a link, is refused with the condition's own sentence ([fatal-halts.md](../errors/fatal-halts.md) §"A reference to another file leads out of the directory it must stay inside"), the error's data placing it on the key in the Release that led to the file, and nothing is read from that file; a Release the configuration names outside the workspace is held the same way to the directory holding it, so a path it or a Release its chain leads to writes that leaves that directory is refused too. Note that `aggrega/releaseCandidates` answers with absolute paths, so a client feeding one surface from the other converts between the two. That this parameter refuses a spelling the per-document `file` and `uri` parameters accept is deliberate, and [Which spellings a parameter you send accepts](#which-spellings-a-parameter-you-send-accepts) says what decides it. The graph withholds every value an author declared sensitive, exactly as `--ir-graph` withholds it on the command line: each is replaced by the marker [`aggrega-inspect`](aggrega-inspect.md#machine-readable-output) "Machine-readable output" describes, and everything else is carried as the compiler recorded it. `unredacted: true` asks for those values in the clear — the protocol's spelling of the command line's `--unredacted`, and the one way to ask; absent or `false`, the answer withholds them. Whatever the answer reaches then carries the values in the clear, so a client asks for them only where the person using it has.

672c67b809dbb1b4: **Schema Agnosticism (open source dictionary):** The core compiler is agnostic to physical execution layers. It does not possess hardcoded schemas for Helm, Terraform, or Docker Compose. Instead, the `source` block of an Ops Recipe is an open dictionary whose keys are provider-defined and surface to the Recipe's templates as `.source.*`. A registry that could not be reached is reported that way too, since no policy came back and the seeding proceeds alike, and carries `unreachable` beside it where the failure itself shows the registry was never reached: its name did not resolve, a connection to it was refused or could not be opened, or a secure connection to it could not be established. A registry that answered — with a not-found, or with an error status — never carries `unreachable`, so read that key rather than the words of `reason` to tell a registry that publishes no policy from one that was never asked. `baseline` means the official hub's built-in baseline was pinned because no advertised policy was taken, with `reason` saying why; the entry carries a policy, so there is nothing to pin by hand. The two keys answer different questions, so a hub that was asked and advertised nothing carries both, and a hub in an offline workspace — never asked — carries `baseline` alone, with `reason` saying the workspace is offline. Any other registry that advertises nothing carries `notAdvertised` alone, is seeded with no policy, and the advice that follows is to pin identities by hand; offline it is refused rather than answered. `skipped` means no fetch was attempted. Every socket runs behind an **AOT-purity firewall**: the host refuses to grant a plugin any runtime-access capability — no network, no filesystem, no wall-clock, no environment, no standard I/O — and rejects a plugin that asks for one. A plugin that cannot reach the network or read the clock cannot break the compiler's ahead-of-time guarantee that the same input produces the same output. Language runtimes that need a few benign startup imports run against a capability-denied configuration of those imports: the host fixes the observable wall clock, supplies real entropy, discards standard I/O, and grants no filesystem, argument, or environment access — so a plugin can reach no host capability that varies across builds. Entropy is deliberately left real rather than pinned: pinning it would stabilise a guest language runtime's internal hash seed and map-iteration order, and so hide a plugin whose own output is not reproducible instead of letting that surface as differing output. A plugin whose result depends on entropy is an authoring-level determinism problem, and this configuration is built to reveal it rather than mask it.

**Stating a rule once: governance attachments are workspace-scoped.**
The two patterns above are authored per component and per Feature, but the governance attachment that enforces them is not. A governance plugin is attached at the workspace configuration's `plugins.governance` key, and that attachment binds **every build in the workspace**. A corporate rule is therefore stated in exactly one place: the platform team attaches the plugin once, and no component, Aggregate or Release has to opt in, mention it, or be edited for it to apply. This is what makes the validation failsafe in pattern 1 a complete answer rather than a per-project convention — a developer who bypasses the internal catalog and requests a naked `core/postgres` is evaluated by the same attached policy as everyone else, because the policy is a property of the workspace rather than of the component they chose.
7000483027a021f9: **Why every catalog YAML repeats the envelope.** The envelope (`apiVersion`, `kind`, `metadata` block) appears at the top of every catalog file — Component, Feature, Recipe, FeatureRecipe, Aggregate, Manifest, Release, Plugin — regardless of how short the body is. The repetition is deliberate: each file is designed to parse, validate, lint, and inspect as a standalone artefact. A single file pulled from the OCI registry, dropped into a CI sandbox, or opened in a third-party editor must carry enough self-description that downstream tooling can identify what kind of entity it represents and which schema version applies. Catalog-relative-path inference (where the directory location implies the entity kind and the envelope could be omitted) is not implemented today — every parser, validator, and linter consumes the envelope explicitly. The cost is mechanical boilerplate per file; the benefit is that the standalone-tooling guarantee holds across the OCI distribution surface, the local filesystem, and the IDE / CI / inspect surfaces. Authors copy the envelope from existing files when authoring new catalog content; future scaffolders are expected to ship the boilerplate as starter templates.
700799c0a0897c89: **The two answers say different things, and that difference is why there are two.** `/healthz` is answered `200` from the moment the process is running, which is the whole of what liveness claims: it is up, and a supervisor that gets no answer at all should restart it. `/readyz` is answered `503` until the workspace this process serves has resolved and the endpoint has bound, and `200` from then on — so a balancer holds traffic back until the process can actually answer a call, rather than sending the first request into one that is still starting. Every answer is a status code with an empty body; no credential is asked for, and nothing the caller sent is read.

7d29cbbb10ba0b7e: **How to fix:** run the pull the message names. For an entry the content cache serves that records no signature where one is required, the pull asks the artifact's registry for its signature, by the manifest digest the entry records, exactly as it does for an artifact it fetches, and records the verified signature on the entry — so the next build reads it. A plugin attached at a verdict role is asked about on every pull in any case, and the pull records what it verified on the plugin's entry in `plugins-trust.yaml`, creating the entry where there is none. A registry that attaches no signature, or a signature the trust configuration does not accept, halts that pull instead, naming the artifact, and that is a question for whoever publishes it. Under the offline posture the pull cannot ask: over a lockfile entry it refuses naming how to allow the network for one run, and over a plugin attached at a verdict role it stops before asking, naming the plugin's `.wasm` as one it could not resolve, because a pull resolves that `.wasm` from the plugin's registry. Restoring the entry's recorded signature from version control clears it without the network, where the cache still holds the signature material that record names. Where the artifact is not meant to be signed, the requirement is the thing to change, and the message names which setting it is — but relaxing it means that registry's artifacts are no longer checked at a pull either, so prefer narrowing the workspace-wide policy's kinds over switching a requirement off.

7d33a7f08d62f9e6: **Connection credential matches target key** (`connection-credential-matches-target-key`) — a server that checks a key holds the key it verifies in a slot of its own Component, and a caller presents a key on the connection it reaches the server through. Neither end sees the other's attachments, so the two hold one key only because their authors write it at both ends — usually by having both attachments read one parameter — and a build never compares them. This rule does, and it is the one rule that reads a whole Release, so it runs under `--release` and at no other scope. It finds both ends by the names the standard catalog gives them: the target's key is the slot `api_key` its Component declares in `spec.featuresSchema`, and the caller's is the slot `credential` on the connection, written at `uses.<socket>.<alias>.features.credential` in the Aggregate or on a connection the Release wires. For each connection whose target declares `api_key` and is not labelled managed, it reports a connection carrying a credential to a target whose key slot is unfilled, a filled key slot with no credential on the connection, and two ends naming their secret differently. What it compares is each end's locator — the `origin` an attachment writes, in `values` in the Aggregate or `infra` in the Release — as the author wrote it, so two ends reading one parameter compare equal and two literals compare by their text; nothing is resolved, and a finding names the component, the connection, the target and the two slots but **never quotes either locator**, since the text written there can be the secret itself. A target declaring no `api_key` slot draws nothing, and a slot that is not the caller key, such as a model server's registry pull token, is never read. Nor is a target whose Component is labelled `component.aggrega.ai/hosting: managed` judged, whatever its `api_key` slot holds: such a Component stands for a service its vendor runs, so nothing the Release runs checks a key on it, and where it declares `api_key` — the key to a hosted model API, say, under the name the vendor's product gives it — the slot holds the key the Release presents to that vendor, never one its callers present. A target labelled `self-hosted`, `external` or `mixed`, or carrying no hosting label, is judged. A connection on the socket `scrape_target` — the name the standard catalog gives the socket a metrics scraper reaches its targets through — is a scrape, and whether a scrape's credential should be the target's caller key depends on the target's product: some serve their metrics with no credential, some put them behind the key every caller presents, and some take a token of their own. So for a scrape the rule reads what the target's Component states in its annotation `observability.aggrega.ai/metrics-credential`: under `none` the scrape is not judged at all; under `separate-token` its credential is never compared with the target's `api_key`, so none of the three findings is reported on it; under `target-key` it is judged like any other connection. The rule reads only those three values, so a scrape to a target without the annotation, or with any other value, is judged like any other connection — and every connection on another socket, a model, tool or datastore connection included, is judged the same whatever the target's annotation says. It reads the attachments written on the target and on the connection: an `api_key` attachment reaching the target from a subsystem or a boundary instead leaves that connection unjudged, one an annotation adds is not among them, so a key slot filled only that way reads as unfilled, an end whose attachment writes no locator is compared only for whether it is filled, and a component an imported module contributes is not read. Because the slot names, the hosting label, the scrape socket's name and the metrics annotation are catalog conventions no schema keyword marks, a catalog naming the slots differently draws nothing, a scraping socket named differently is judged like any other socket, and a Component that holds a vendor's key in a slot named `api_key` without the managed label is read as a target checking that key, since the slot's name, the label and the annotation are all the rule reads of a target's Component. Default on; opt out with `allow_connection_credential_mismatches`.

**The Golden Rule for Ops Recipes (The Helm Pattern):**
Platform Ops engineers must **never** hardcode physical cloud resource names. Instead, they must construct deterministically unique names by concatenating the Aggrega deployment context during the template evaluation phase. This is a **reusability and collision-safety rule**, not a determinism rule — hardcoded names produce stable output but fatally collide when the same Recipe renders multiple component instances or when the same Aggregate deploys across multiple Releases.

8d21332250ee1308: **Which plugins are pinned, and which your environment chooses.** Aggrega splits plugins by whether they change the output you ship. Output-shaping plugins — the render providers, the mutator, and the FeatureRecipe and Recipe pipeline steps — are pinned in the release lockfile when you `aggrega pull`, and reproduced byte-identically at `aggrega build` and `aggrega serve` from that lockfile alone. Two kinds are not pinned, because a build reads each from the same place every time: a render provider served from inside the compiler binary, and a provider or pipeline step whose `Plugin` entity is authored in one of your own catalog directories. To change which output-shaping plugin applies, you re-pull; a change to your workspace configuration after a pull does not move a build's output until the next pull. Gate plugins — policy and lint — judge a build without changing its bytes, so they are cached at pull (so a build can still run them offline; one the compiler binary carries, or one authored in your own catalog directory, is read from there instead) but not pinned: which gate runs is chosen by your environment at build time, so a dev-permissive / CI-strict split is an ordinary configuration choice rather than a re-pull, and switching gates never changes the output a passing build emits. **Centralized Enterprise Governance (Evaluating Complete Reality):**
Relying on out-of-band mechanisms (like `CODEOWNERS` on a git repository) to govern architecture is a weak workaround. All governance is localized in the compiler's governance verdict roles. Because the AOT compiler builds the IR Graph by flattening *both* the Developer's `Aggregate` and the Ops Engineer's `Release`, the policy engine evaluates the complete reality before physical artifacts are generated. Policies can fatally halt the build if a developer requests an unapproved Component, if Ops maps a component to an unapproved Recipe in the Manifest, or if an insecure Wasm mutation is attached to a Component carrying a `restricted` subsystem label.

The write is atomic, so a client reading that file while the alignment runs never observes a partial document.

It is encapsulated within the Platform Catalog through specialized `components`, `features`, and `recipes`. Developers preserve their specific application intent within their `values` and `uses` blocks — strictly governed by the Architect's `schema:` declarations (compact form or full JSON Schema 2020-12) — while the physical translation of that intelligence is executed by target-specific WebAssembly plugins.

925a286772cae701: **Resilience:** `core/fallback-chain` sends a request whose model fails on to other models: `chains` names, for each model alias that falls back, the aliases to try in order until one answers, a fallback that fails following its own entry in turn, and `max_hops` bounds how far along that chain a request is passed. The standard library realizes it on the AI gateway by writing both into the routing configuration the gateway's Recipe renders, and halts the build on a name the gateway's model map does not publish. A request falls back only once the gateway has given up on the alias it asked for: where one alias is published more than once, a failed call first moves to another of its entries as a retry, bounded by the gateway's retry count. `core/retry-policy` sets that count — how many times the gateway may send a request, the first send included (`max_attempts`), for a failure that succeeds on being sent again, such as a refused connection, a rate limit or a timeout — and the standard library realizes it on the AI gateway by writing it into the routing configuration the gateway's Recipe renders. On `core/gateway/envoy-gateway` it is realized as the retry of the traffic policy on the route serving the wired models, the same policy that carries a period budget's rate limit, because Envoy Gateway attaches one traffic policy to a route: a request is sent again after a refused connection or stream, a reset or a reply of 429, 503 or 504, up to `max_attempts` sends, and a model that answers nothing within the route's request timeout is not sent again, because that timeout spans every send. On `core/gateway/azure-api-management` it is realized as Azure's retry around the forwarding, in the backend section of the API's policy: a request answered with HTTP 429 or a 5xx status is sent again, its body held so it can be resent, one second after the previous send, up to `max_attempts` sends. A refused or dropped connection, and a model that answers nothing within the forwarding's timeout, are not sent again, because Azure ends the retry on such an error and hands it to the policy's on-error section. Azure retries 1 to 50 times after the first send, so a `max_attempts` of 1 writes no retry and one above 51 is refused by name. The retry takes the place of the forwarding the API would inherit, so while it is attached a forwarding setting made at a broader scope of the instance, such as a timeout, does not apply to the API, which forwards with Azure's defaults. On the hosted gateway, `core/retry-policy` is realized by writing into the gateway's resource its retry count, which names the sends after the first, from 1 to 5, so `max_attempts` from 2 to 6 is honoured and any other value refused; `core/fallback-chain` is not realized there, because that gateway falls back between models only inside a route a request names in place of a model, so a request for a model never falls back. On `core/gateway/kong-enterprise`, `core/fallback-chain` is realized on its chart Recipe: the chat and completion routes of each alias `chains` gives an entry carry Kong's AI Proxy Advanced in place of its AI proxy, with the alias's model and the models its walk falls back to as targets in priority order — the alias, then its entry's fallbacks in order, a fallback's own entry followed in turn only while fewer than `max_hops` have been counted. The balancer sends a request to each target of the walk once, in order, until one answers, moving on after a connection error or timeout, an invalid reply header or a reply of 429, 500, 502, 503 or 504, and returns every other reply as it came. The build halts on a name the `models` socket does not carry, on a walk reaching an alias twice, beside `core/retry-policy`, since Kong keeps one retry count for the whole walk and cannot send to a model again before falling back, and on a gateway image older than 3.12. `core/retry-policy` is not realized there, and its realization halts every attachment naming why: each wired model is served on routes of its own carrying that one model, so a retry has to send the request to that same target again, and Kong's reference reads both ways on whether its balancer does. On `core/gateway/agentgateway`, `core/retry-policy` is realized on the chart Recipe as a retry policy of the gateway's own configuration, attached to the listener its model requests arrive on: a request is sent again, at once and to the same model, after a reply of 429, 500, 502, 503 or 504, a refused or reset connection, a connection taking longer than 11 seconds to open or a failed name lookup, up to `max_attempts` sends. agentgateway sends a request once more than its policy's attempts, so the policy is written as `max_attempts` less one, `max_attempts` 1 writes none, and one above 256 is refused by name. A request whose body is larger than 64 KiB is sent once, and the configuration sets no timeout, so a model that accepts the connection and answers nothing is waited on rather than sent again. `core/fallback-chain` is not realized there, and its realization halts every attachment naming why: agentgateway fails over between models by evicting a failed one for the requests after it, while the request that failed is answered with its failure, so no request is walked along a chain. On `core/gateway/higress`, `core/retry-policy` is realized as the route's own retry, written as Ingress annotations onto every model route: a request is sent again after a refused or reset connection, a 5xx reply or a 429, a POST included, up to `max_attempts` sends; `max_attempts` 1 writes the retry off, overriding the retry Higress's control plane gives a route carrying no annotation, and one above 2147483648 is refused by name. A model that accepts the connection and then answers nothing or slowly is not sent again, since the route sets no per-try deadline, and a streamed request is sent again only before its reply has begun. `core/fallback-chain` is not realized there either, and its realization halts every attachment naming why: Higress sends a failed request on at most once, to one other destination — a route's default backend, or the one fallback route its console writes for an AI route — so no request is walked along a chain. On `core/gateway/traefik-hub` both are realized on the chart Recipe, and each halts the build on a Traefik Hub image older than v3.20, whose failover takes no middlewares on the services it tries and whose retry cannot send a POST again on a reply's status — a retry policy of one send excepted. `core/fallback-chain` sends the route of each alias `chains` gives an entry through nested failovers of Traefik's own, trying the models of the alias's walk in order — the alias, then its entry's fallbacks in order, a fallback's own entry followed in turn only while fewer than `max_hops` have been counted — each with its own model name, credential, quotas and retry. A model's reply of 429 or of 500 to 504, after any retry of that model, moves the request on to the next; any other reply is returned as it came, the last model's whatever it is, and a request body over 1 MiB is refused with HTTP 413 rather than sent. The build halts on a name the `models` socket does not carry and on a walk reaching an alias twice. `core/retry-policy` is Traefik's retry middleware, last on each model route, or on each model a walk tries: a request is sent again at once after a connection that carried nothing to the model and after a reply of 429 or of 500 to 504, a POST included, up to `max_attempts` sends, the first included, and `max_attempts` 1 writes nothing. A reply the gateway forms itself — a refusal of its key check, a guard, the masking or a quota — is never sent again, and neither is a streamed reply once it has begun.

**Action:** The CLI fetches all requested entities (Components, Features, Releases). It first checks these definitions for the `extends` keyword. For the Catalog entities, it deep-merges the YAML metadata, and the two kinds part company on the data pillars: a Feature's `schema:` composes with its base's under JSON Schema 2020-12 composition, while an extending Component composes structure only — its attachment slots, topology sockets, self-inject allowlist and named assertions — and receives its base's `schema:` block exactly as the base authored it. An extending `Release` folds by the same rule: the child's value wins key by key, down to the first indivisible value — a scalar, a list, a template — which replaces whole, and a key the child writes as `null` is removed. So its whole authoring surface travels — the boundary tree with its per-component `infra` and Feature attachments, the `parameters` block, the annotations, and the Manifest pointer — while no `metadata` field does, since identity and provenance are per-Release.
Next, it performs an in-memory interpolation in three sub-steps: parameter contract validation against the Aggregate's typed `parameters:` declarations; interpolation of the resolved values into the surrounding `values:` strings; withdrawal of the `.parameters` map from every value-template context, leaving it readable to operator-authored path templates alone. Finally, it injects the resolved `infra` blocks into the target component payloads. Once the blueprint is fully concrete, the compiler uses the unified `schema:` declaration from the Catalog (compact form or full JSON Schema 2020-12) to strictly validate the developer's `values` and `infra` configurations locally.

It attaches to any component declaring `dataplane.aggrega.ai/period-budget`. The standard library realizes it on the AI gateway, whose budget covers everything the gateway serves, is counted in US dollars, and starts again at the start of every period — a number of days from midnight UTC, or a calendar month from its first day: the realization writes the limit and the period into the configuration the gateway's Recipe renders, refuses any other unit, scope or period by name — `30d` among them, which the gateway counts as a calendar month — and halts unless the gateway's `database_url` and `api_key` credential slots are both attached, because without its bookkeeping database the gateway keeps no count and without an administrative key it checks no caller against the budget. Once the count exceeds the limit, the gateway refuses the administrative key's model requests as well as every caller's; its model listing and key management still answer that key. On the hosted gateway it is realized as a spend-limit rule on the gateway's resource, counted in US dollars over a window that moves forward with time — the last `period`, for models whose pricing the gateway knows — for everything the gateway serves: a budget per caller or per model, tokens and a calendar month are refused by name. Once the count reaches the limit the gateway answers model requests with HTTP 503 until the window closes; a request's tokens are added once its reply completes, so the request that reaches the limit is served, and a reply its semantic cache serves counts nothing and is served past the limit. APISIX counts no tokens on a completion request, so while the budget is attached each wired model gets its chat route alone, and it keeps the count in the memory of the gateway process, so the chart runs one replica and a restart opens a new window. On `core/gateway/envoy-gateway` it is realized as Envoy Gateway's usage-based rate limit, on the AI route serving the models wired to the gateway: the route declares the token count `unit` names — `total_tokens`, `prompt_tokens` or `completion_tokens` — as a cost Envoy AI Gateway reads off each reply, and a traffic policy on that route charges it when the reply completes, against `limit` tokens per one unit of Envoy Gateway's rate limit, for everything the gateway serves or for each wired model apart. aa0d4bdb67cbd9f0: **Semantic caching:** `core/semantic-caching` declares a cache that answers a prompt with the reply stored for an earlier one close enough in meaning, rather than calling the model again. `embedding_model` names the model that turns each prompt into a vector, as the gateway publishes it, a stored reply is served when the two prompts are at least `similarity_threshold` alike, and it stays usable for `ttl_seconds`. `scope` decides who shares a cache: `end_user`, the default, keeps each end user the gateway identifies apart, while `key` serves every caller presenting one key from one cache, so an end user behind that key can be served a reply generated for another. It does not meet `core/data-masking` on one component. The standard library realizes it on the AI gateway, which keeps the replies in a `core/datastore/redis` wired to its `cache_store` socket, presenting to the store the password the credential on that connection holds where the store requires one, the store removing each reply once `ttl_seconds` have passed, and caches chat, responses and messages requests, not completions or embeddings. The realization halts the build unless the gateway's `api_key` slot is attached, because without an administrative key the gateway checks no caller, on an `embedding_model` the gateway's model map does not publish, and when nothing is wired to `cache_store`. A stored reply is served only to a request matching what it was stored under: the key the request presents, which the gateway verifies, with that key's team and organization; under `end_user`, the end user the request names; and the model the request asks for with its other parameters. The gateway writes the key, team, organization and end user into the request itself, over any value a caller sent for them on a chat request; on a responses or messages request it removes a team, organization or end user field from the request's own metadata and refuses one naming the key there, so no request can name its way into another key's replies. A request's own metadata can still move it among the replies of the key it presents: on a responses request `model_group` replaces the model it asks for in what its reply is stored under; on a responses or messages request `caching_groups` lets requests naming the same group of model aliases share replies across them; and on a responses or chat request `redis_namespace` keeps requests naming a namespace apart from those naming none. The gateway reads an end user from a header or a body field the request itself names, and verifies none of them: under `end_user` a caller naming another end user is served that end user's replies, and requests naming no end user share one cache with every other such request under the key they present. The hosted gateway does not realize it: its cache answers only a request identical to an earlier one. On `core/gateway/azure-api-management` it is realized as Azure's semantic cache lookup and store, written into the API's policy: `embedding_model` names a backend the API Management instance already holds for an embeddings model, which the instance reaches with its managed identity, and the instance needs a Redis cache with RediSearch configured as its external cache, neither of which the build can see, so the build halts until the operator affirms that the cache serves RediSearch by setting the gateway's `infra.cache_serves_vector_search`; the store keeps a reply for `ttl_seconds`; and `similarity_threshold` is written as Azure's score threshold, one minus the threshold, reading that score as a cosine distance, since Microsoft gives its range and its direction — lower requires closer prompts — but not its measure. A reply is stored and served apart per API and per API Management subscription, whose key the gateway verifies, so the realization keeps `key`, refuses it on an API that requires no subscription key, and refuses `end_user`: the API its Recipe renders validates no end user's token, so the gateway has no verified end user to keep apart. Nor do `core/gateway/contour` and `core/gateway/nginx`, which offer no semantic cache. On `core/gateway/agentgateway` its realization halts every attachment, naming why: agentgateway keeps no cache of replies, and its prompt caching only marks where a provider that caches prompts itself may do so. On `core/gateway/kong-enterprise` its realization halts every attachment, naming the scope asked for: Kong's AI Semantic Cache has no setting that keeps one caller's stored replies apart from another's, and the gateway tells callers apart only as the consumers an authentication plugin names and declares no callers, for the reasons "Kong in front of models" above gives, so under `end_user` and under `key` alike every request would share one cache. On `core/gateway/higress` its realization halts every attachment, naming the scope asked for: Higress's semantic cache stores each reply under one key prefix followed by the prompt text, and nothing in that key names a caller or an end user, while the gateway declares no callers, so every request would share one cache. On `core/gateway/apisix` it is realized on the chart Recipe, written onto each wired model's chat route as APISIX 3.18.0's semantic cache, for the callers its Release declares in `infra.callers`: a reply is stored per route and per caller, under the key the caller presented, which the gateway verifies, so no caller is served a reply stored for another; the realization keeps `key` and refuses `end_user` by name, because the gateway cannot tell apart the end users behind one key. `embedding_model` names a connection on the gateway's `models` socket, whose endpoint, model and credential the cache embeds with. The cache embeds a request's last user message and serves a stored reply whose message is at least `similarity_threshold` alike and whose earlier messages — a system prompt, earlier turns — are the same. The replies sit for `ttl_seconds` in a `core/datastore/redis` wired to the gateway's `cache_store` socket, to which the cache presents the password the credential on that connection holds, and a reply served by meaning is stored again under that request for `ttl_seconds` more. Completion requests are not cached, and a store or embedding failure is a miss: the request is still answered. The realization halts with no caller declared, with nothing wired to `cache_store` or to the `models` socket, and on an `embedding_model` no connection there carries. APISIX keys a stored reply by route and caller rather than by gateway, so two APISIX gateways wired to one store, or two Releases of one Aggregate pointing their gateway at one external store, can serve a cached reply to a caller of the same name on the same alias and model. Its workload Recipe, at APISIX 3.17.0, carries no semantic cache at all. On `core/gateway/traefik-hub` it is realized on the chart Recipe as Traefik Hub's semantic cache on the route of each wired model, for the callers its Release declares in `infra.callers`: a reply is stored per wired model and per caller, under the caller the gateway's key check verified, each by its own key, so no caller is served a reply stored for another; the realization keeps `key` and refuses `end_user` by name, because the gateway cannot tell apart the end users behind one key. `embedding_model` names a connection on the gateway's `models` socket, whose endpoint, model and credential the cache embeds a request's text with. `similarity_threshold` is written as the cache's distance bound, one minus the threshold, read as a cosine distance, since Traefik's reference gives the bound's direction but not its measure. A reply is kept for `ttl_seconds` in a `core/datastore/redis` wired to the gateway's `cache_store` socket, and a request too large to embed is answered uncached. The realization halts with no caller declared, with nothing wired to `cache_store` or to the `models` socket, on an `embedding_model` no connection there carries, and on a Traefik Hub image whose tag names no release from v3.19.11 within 3.19 or from v3.20.6, since an earlier release shares one cache among every caller of a route.

That is the most useful answer the operation gives, and it arrives as a result rather than as a failure precisely so you can show the author both halves. Under `sync` the same answer writes nothing — `files`, `written` and `drift` are empty — because a partial draft would read as a source that dropped every part the importer did not reach. **Domain 2: The Split Schema (`usesSchema` & `schema`)**
To prevent the Platform Catalog from fragmenting into unmanageable schema files, Aggrega utilizes a Split Schema engine. The Native YAML `usesSchema` strictly defines and validates the topology, while `schema:` (JSON Schema 2020-12 — typically authored via the compact-form shorthand) validates the content of the `values` and `infra` pillars and declares the shape of the `provides` pillar. The `values` a developer authors and the `infra` an operator sets are checked against their declared types; the `provides` sub-schema declares the key names and types of the downstream contract a Recipe produces, and the compiler checks that every `inject` reference names a declared `provides` key — but the produced `provides` values themselves travel downstream as opaque strings the compiler pipes without interpretation, not values it type-checks, because the core does not interpret what a piped value means. **The `usesSchema` is where a socket is *declared*, and declaring one is what gives it a contract.** A socket the catalog entity declares carries that entity's constraints: a selector saying which targets it may reach, an `inject` allowlist, and per-edge `valueSchema` / `infraSchema`. Inside the `usesSchema`, Platform Architects use the `selector:` field — read as the string the Architect wrote, not copied into any generated schema — and the native Go selector engine evaluates it to enforce **Cross-Node Type Safety** over declared sockets. It ensures that if a socket requires a database, the developer cannot plug in a web server.

One declaring no `apiVersion` at all is reported, being an Aggrega document with a field missing rather than another project's file. `list-releases` searches no directory outside the workspace root, so a Release your editor shows under a link leading to one is not listed; `unread_linked_dirs` names each link that stands where the listing would read a directory and leads outside the root — by the link's own path relative to the root, never by where it leads — in both shapes and on both transports, and is empty where there is none. Deprecating an artifact writes to the registry twice: the marker, attached as a
referrer of the artifact, and then the marker's signature, attached as a referrer
of the marker. Each write is retried when the registry or the network fails it in
a way a later attempt can succeed, such as a server error, a timeout or a reset
connection; [`aggrega push`](aggrega-push.md#when-the-registry-fails-a-write)
lists those failures. A write is tried at most three times, half a second and then
a second apart, and each attempt is a new upload of the same bytes rather than a
resend of the request that failed. The marker's timestamp is stamped once, before
the first attempt, so a retried write leaves one marker and one signature, not two.

c334b62249151054: The three identifiers carry their stability separately, and that separation is the reason a condition has all three. The accessors listed below are stable across patch releases; renames or removals are signalled by a release-notes entry and a deprecation cycle, and adding a new accessor within a package is additive and does not break existing matchers. A code is fixed once its condition is published, so it is the identifier to record wherever a condition has to be named durably: renaming an accessor does not move the code its condition was registered under, and a code you have recorded outlives a refactor of the Go surface. A short code is the most durable of the three: a number is handed out once and then fixed, and a retired condition's number stays retired rather than being handed to a different condition, so a short code recorded in an old report still names the condition it named when it was recorded. That is enforced rather than merely intended — a condition declared under a retired number is refused before the compiler reads any input, on every run — and every retired number is published beside the live ones in [the table of every condition](#every-condition-by-short-code). The code column below carries the code, and it is the value a client of the structured diagnostic reads without linking these packages. It is published rather than inferred, because it need not restate the row it sits on — a re-exported name reports the code of the condition it forwards to, and a rule's code names the rule rather than the accessor. The message column is the literal text the sentinel renders; the user-facing diagnostic puts a bracketed head and the source location ahead of that text.
