c9c02f14b90c1cea: **Caller-Identity Propagation, at two hops:** The original caller's identity has to survive two different hops, and each is protected at a different place. At the **gateway hop**, the developer attaches `core/context-propagation` to the gateway a request enters through, which selects on `dataplane.aggrega.ai/caller-identity`. At **compile-time**, the attachment is realized in that gateway's own configuration — on Envoy Gateway, a client traffic policy that verifies each client's certificate against an authority the Release names and forwards the certificate's details; on the LiteLLM AI gateway, a request hook that removes any identity header a caller supplied and adds the user and team of the virtual key the gateway verified, and its organization where the key names one, on requests to the model aliases the attachment lists in `destinations`. At **runtime**, the service behind the gateway receives who called rather than only that the gateway called. At the **workload hop**, a request one agent makes directly to another never crosses that gateway, so it is checked at the receiving agent's own ingress, where a service mesh rejects any request lacking a signed token proving the original user's intent (e.g., an Istio JWT `AuthorizationPolicy`). The standard library ships the gateway-hop Feature and no workload-hop Feature, so attaching `core/context-propagation` protects the traffic that passes through a gateway and leaves agent-to-agent calls to mesh configuration the enterprise supplies itself. An agent another party runs, which `core/ai-tool/agent-invocation` reaches over A2A as `core/ai-agent/a2a-remote`, sits outside the Release altogether: that party checks each call against the security scheme the agent's Agent Card declares, and the tool presents the credential held on its connection, read from a Secret by reference, under the request header the agent publishes. Where the card requires OAuth 2.0 client credentials or OpenID Connect, the connection holds a client secret instead, or as well, with the client id the operator writes on it, and the agent publishes the token or discovery address and the scopes its card declares; the tool's own container obtains the token with them, refreshes it and presents it on each call; the catalog delivers only those inputs, and no build can check what the container does with them. Where the card requires mutual TLS, the connection holds a client certificate, and, where an authority the image does not already trust signs the agent's server certificate, that authority too; each is mounted into the tool's container as files from a Secret the connection names, and the container presents the certificate in the TLS handshake itself. So the tool reaches an agent whose card declares an API key in a header or a cookie, an HTTP authentication scheme whose value is fixed, such as Bearer or Basic, with the Secret holding the whole header value, OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect with the client-credentials grant, or mutual TLS. It does not reach one whose card requires a key in the query string, an HTTP scheme answering a challenge from the agent, such as Digest, or an OAuth 2.0 flow other than client credentials. Nor does it present a credential to an agent another party runs over plain HTTP: where that agent's address is `http`, a credential or a client secret on the connection halts the build, naming the connection, because the credential, or the token obtained with the secret, would travel to it unencrypted. An agent running inside the Release stays reachable over `http` with either, and the credential then crosses the cluster network unencrypted.

**Directories listed under `workspace.catalog_dirs` are read as well, and they are read first.**
The list is an ordered search stack: the first directory to declare an identity owns it, and the
same identity in a later directory is shadowed. `catalog` is read after everything listed — unless
a listed directory already contains it, in which case it is read as part of that directory — so
listing a directory adds to what you had rather than replacing it. A repeatable `--catalog <dir>`
on the command line is read ahead of both, and a relative path given there resolves against the
directory you ran the command from, since no configuration file declared it. A directory named more
than once — on the command line and in the list, or twice in the list — is read once, at the place it
was first named, so nothing in it is reported as shadowed by itself: a shadow is always two different
files declaring one identity. Two spellings of one directory, a path to it through a link, and — on a
file system that ignores case — a spelling in another case all name that one directory. A directory
inside another listed directory is still read as its own entry. A project that keeps a
catalog variant per Release can give each Release a list of its own instead — see
[Giving a Release its own catalog directories](#giving-a-release-its-own-catalog-directories).

**The requests that go out to a registry divide into the ones that read and the ones that publish.**
`aggrega/resolveDependencies` fetches what a Release needs, and
`aggrega/build` joins it when — and only when — its `autoPull` field asks it to resolve
dependencies first, in which case it reaches a registry and writes the lockfile before it renders;
`aggrega/registryUpdate` walks every configured registry to rebuild the local search index;
`aggrega/pluginAdd` searches the configured registry for the plugin a request names and reads its
published versions to pin one; `aggrega/registryAdd` asks the registry it registers for the trust
policy that registry advertises, unless the request declines the fetch or supplies a policy of its
own, and `aggrega/configInit` asks the registry it is seeding for the same; `aggrega/explainError` acquires the documentation bundle it reads
a condition's walk-through from, once, where the cache every project on the machine shares holds no copy the
workspace's own signature check admits — see [`aggrega explain`](aggrega-explain.md);
`aggrega/import` fetches a core importer from the workspace's default registry, once, where the
machine does not hold it yet — see [What an import response tells you](#what-an-import-response-tells-you); and
`aggrega/entityDefinition` reads the entity a registry reference names when one is sent as its `name`,
writing nothing.
`aggrega/publishEntity`, `aggrega/publishArtifact`, `aggrega/signArtifacts` and
`aggrega/deprecateArtifact` write to one — bytes, a signature, or a withdrawal marker. A request
reaches a registry only when it was sent to do that: a listing reports what the configuration pins, a
search reads an offline snapshot, and a publication asked for with `dryRun` computes what it would
send and contacts nobody.

Typed as `--release release.yaml` where `release.yaml` is a link to a file kept elsewhere — or named
that way under `workspace.releases`, or as `build.authoring_release` — the Release is read from the

for beside the link, in the directory you named it in, and held to that directory's root: the
workspace, or the directory itself where it lies outside the workspace. Its lockfile is read and
written beside the link too, never where the link leads. The Release is not one of the documents its
own lookup meets beside it, so it never stops that lookup; another Release kept beside it that is a
link leading out still does. A Manifest you inspect on its own through a link is read and resolved
the same way.

dbc0f2ee86410882: **Concurrency:** `core/concurrency-limit` caps how many requests a gateway carries at once (`max_in_flight`), which keeps a burst of callers from becoming a queue at the model behind it. `scope` says what one cap counts: `gateway`, the default, counts every request the gateway forwards together; `model` gives each target the gateway sends requests to a count of its own, a target being each upstream entry the gateway routes to, so where one model name has several entries each is counted apart. The cap and its scope are capacity sizing the operator decides, set in the attachment's `infra`, so the operator attaches it in the Release. The cap is counted per running proxy, so where several replicas run each of them admits that many. It attaches to any component declaring `dataplane.aggrega.ai/concurrency-cap`, and a realization refuses by name the scope its gateway does not count. On `core/gateway/nginx` scope `gateway` is realized as NGINX's `limit_conn`, keyed on one word the same for every request, so NGINX counts every request it is processing as one total, kept in memory its worker processes share, and answers a request past the cap with HTTP 503; scope `model` is refused, since NGINX keeps no count for each upstream target, and so is a `max_in_flight` above 65535, the most `limit_conn` takes. On `core/gateway/envoy-gateway` scope `model` is realized as the circuit breaker of the traffic policy on the route serving the wired models, the policy that also carries a period budget's rate limit and the retry policy's retry: Envoy Gateway applies it to the backend of each rule of that route, and each wired model has a rule of its own, so at most `max_in_flight` requests are sent to each wired model at once, and a request past the cap is answered with HTTP 503 and is not sent again; a send the retry policy repeats counts against the cap like the first. Envoy's worker threads check the count and then add to it, so requests arriving together can take it briefly above the cap. Scope `gateway` is refused, since Envoy Gateway keeps a cap for each backend and none on their total, and so is an attachment with nothing wired to the `models` socket. On the AI gateway scope `model` is realized as the `max_parallel_requests` of every entry of its model map, typed by hand and wired alike: at most `max_in_flight` requests are in flight to each entry at once, and a request finding its entry full is answered with HTTP 429 — after the gateway's retries where its alias has one entry, and at once where it has several, even while another of them has room, since the proxy picks the entry before it counts — unless `core/fallback-chain` lists fallbacks for its alias, to which it is then sent on. The proxy keeps each count in memory, where by default a record lapses ten minutes after it is made and a new count then starts at zero, so the attachment also sets that lifetime to a century, keeping every count as long as the proxy runs. Because of that lifetime the gateway refuses a request carrying `priority` while the cap is attached, even where the Release admits the field, since the proxy keeps a queue entry for every such request until its record lapses; and the build halts on a model map of more than 100 entries, past which the store the counts are kept in, which holds 200 records and drops one whenever it is full, could drop a count. Scope `gateway` is refused there, since the proxy's one total is read only by a request limiter an environment variable switches on, which counts a request for its first second. Nor does the hosted gateway realize it: the request limit its terraform Recipe writes into the gateway's resource is a rate, a number of requests over an interval, rather than a cap on the requests in flight.

de47c5b09f6f21ee: **The bundle owns its filenames, and the consuming key owns the directory they land in.** One `artifacts:` entry importing a bundle expands into one output per file in that bundle, each nested under the consumption key as `<key>/<filename>`. The key at the consumption site — `operator-support` above — names the whole consumption rather than any single file; the example emits `operator-support/crd.yaml` and `operator-support/rbac.yaml`. So a bundle name is chosen for legibility at the reference, the filenames are chosen for the reader of the output directory, and neither has to agree with the other. The consumption key is itself bounded to a single filename — a leading letter or digit, then letters, digits, dots, hyphens and underscores, with a key outside that alphabet failing envelope validation — so it names exactly one directory segment, and everything below that segment comes from the bundle. That is what lets a bundle's filenames stay free-form while the key stays strict: a filename is unique within its bundle, a key is unique within its document, and the key is the first segment of every path the entry emits, so no two `artifacts:` entries name one output. Free-form means free within that segment: a filename may carry a nested layout of its own — `crds/widget.yaml` lands at `<key>/crds/widget.yaml` — but it must be an ordinary relative file name beneath the key, written plainly, and a filename that is not one halts the build instead of placing the file somewhere the consuming Recipe never named. That refuses a name climbing above the key or naming an absolute location; `.` or `./`, and a name that collapses back onto the key such as `x/..`, which name the key's own directory rather than a file in it; and a name with a trailing or doubled `/` or a `.` or `..` part — `x/`, `a//b`, `./a`, `a/../b` — which is a second spelling of a file another name can carry, so `a//b` beside `a/b` would put two files at one path. The diagnostic names the bundle file and the key it was imported at. Two outputs that do carry the same filename halt the build when the node renders, which happens when two different input kinds contribute one filename. **(D) The Dynamic Business Context (Cascading Annotations)**
While `labels` define the immutable Catalog DNA, dynamic business contexts (like SOC2 audit scoping or FinOps cost tracking) change depending on who deploys the application and where it runs. These are governed by **Annotations** injected dynamically by the Developer's `subsystems`, the Ops `Release` boundaries, or the governance `label-transform` auto-tagger.

e782f0cba91d7cb2: **The check follows an alias for the block.** A key reached through the dot a `with .locals` body rebinds, or through a variable bound to `.locals`, is checked on exactly the terms the direct spelling gets: `{{ with .locals }}{{ .nope }}{{ end }}` and `{{ $l := .locals }}{{ $l.nope }}` both halt naming `.locals.nope`, just as `{{ .locals.nope }}` does. One is a key reached through a call whose result the template text cannot name — `{{ index .locals "nope" }}` — because what such a call yields is decided when the template runs rather than by what is written. The other is a key read off a parenthesised block — `{{ (.locals).nope }}` or `{{ ($.locals).nope }}` — where the key hangs off the value the parentheses yield rather than off the block itself. **Only the router's own routes are reachable.** The guard sees only the routes
that hand it the request, so the second ConfigMap's other file configures the
pod's second container, which mounts that ConfigMap alone and runs the official
nginx image as a path allowlist. The router itself listens on the pod's
loopback address, where nothing outside the pod reaches it, and the allowlist
listens on port 4000, the port the Service below targets. It forwards a request
only when its method and path are one of the routes the router serves — the
model request routes the guard checks, in the spellings the router serves
whatever the alias, `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/messages` among them; the
model listing; the health checks; and, of its
administrative routes, key management — and answers every other path 403,
forwarding nothing. So the proxy's token-count routes, its pass-through routes to
providers' own APIs, its other administrative routes and its administrative
console cannot be reached through the router, and neither can a model route
whose path carries the model name, as the paths Azure's client sends do:
there the proxy reads words in the path, the alias included, to decide how it
records a request, and the router would refuse a request for this map's own
`assistant` on it. The proxy's metrics are not among those routes either: port
4000 answers `/metrics` 403. With the router's `metrics_enabled` true, as the
Aggregate sets it, the allowlist also listens on port 9090 and forwards a GET of
`/metrics` there alone, to the listener the proxy keeps for its metrics on the
loopback address, answering every other request 403. That port checks no
caller, and the metrics name the hashed keys, key aliases and user emails the
router attributes spend to.

f509e371715df0db: **The plugin whose rules are read is the one serving the capability in your workspace when you pin**: your workspace's provider binding for that capability, or else the plugin built into `aggrega`. The step records that plugin — its reference and the digest of its entity — and the exact rules it composed in the `entity.lock`. From then on, every reading of the directory applies the recorded rules and no others: a publication of the entity, the comparison a pull or a push holds the lock to, the entity's row in a lockfile, a build's comparison, the render that hands the directory to a provider, and `aggrega pull --verify`. So what you publish is exactly what your own build renders, and a changed binding, an edited `.aggregaignore` or a newer `aggrega` changes nothing until you pin again — at which point the lock's diff shows what moved. A file a plugin names as an ignore file, such as a `.helmignore`, is itself one of the source's files and is pinned like any other unless a rule leaves it out, so editing it without pinning again is caught by the next pull or build. A lock that records no rules keeps every file under the directory.

**4. Ops Domain: The FeatureRecipe (Wasm Pipeline)**
The FeatureRecipe maps the abstract Feature to a concrete Wasm plugin pipeline. The pipeline executes sequentially in the plugin pipeline that closes rendering: this one patches the configuration the gateway's own Recipe already renders rather than emitting a file of its own. The plugin pipeline runs during `aggrega build`; see [Status of the Language](../10-status.md#compilation-pipeline-phases).
f7ac94a1ef6870b8: The reason is consumption-surface uniformity. Recipes and FeatureRecipes are Go-template throughout, and their own content evaluates through the same Go template engine that resolves an imported bundle. A parallel authoring surface would force authors to switch evaluation models within a single Recipe's rendering — one model for the Recipe's own content, another for any imported bundle. Keeping the surface uniform means authors learn one evaluation model and apply it everywhere.

  lockfile and fetches it into a content-addressed cache; `aggrega build` renders
  from that cache, so lock-time and build-time resolve the same chart. The chart

  resolution). The per-release lockfiles pin entity identities and digests:
